title: Tilaurakot (Kapilavastu candidate), Nepal
summary: Walled early-historic city in Nepal's Terai, one of two rival candidates for Kapilavastu, the Shakya capital of Buddhist tradition. Excavation by Nepal and Durham University dates first occupation to the 8th century BCE, fortification to the 6th, and abandonment of the core in the first half of the first millennium CE.

uncertainty.note: Start is the first occupation dated at the Samai Mai Temple trench (8th century BCE, "new dates suggest"). End is the "first half of the first millennium CE" abandonment of the city core; the interval is wide.

as_recorded.value: first occupied in the eighth century BCE; fortified in the sixth century BCE; core largely abandoned in the first half of the first millennium CE
brick-lined water tank constructed in the third century BCE

when.display: Occupied from the 8th century BCE; fortified in the 6th century BCE; core abandoned by the mid first millennium CE

where.modern_name: Tilaurakot-Kapilavastu, near Taulihawa, Kapilvastu District, Lumbini Province, Nepal
where.historical_name: Walled city in the Shakya country (identification with Kapilavastu is disputed); later within Mauryan territory

importance.justification: Best-planned excavated early-historic city in the Buddha's homeland and a leading candidate for his childhood home.

perspectives.account: Tilaurakot-Kapilavastu is the Shakya capital and the Buddha's childhood home, as P. C. Mukherji argued in 1898-99.
Piprahwa, just across the border in Uttar Pradesh, is the other main contender for ancient Kapilavastu.

reviewer_note: Identification with Kapilavastu is contested (Piprahwa is the rival). Durham says the citadel is about 500 by 400 m and the site is 3 km north of Taulihawa; Wikidata supplies the point. "Shakya capital" is tradition, as is the Mahapajapati link (the Buddha's stepmother).
